issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment governing pre-emption suits requires a pending appeal to be decided under the amended law, so a decree based on a pre-emption right removed by the amendment cannot stand.
material_facts: The respondents’ pre-emption suits had been decreed under provisions that recognized their claimed right, and those decrees were under appeal.
While the appeals were pending, an amendment deleted the provisions on which the decrees rested and directed that no decree inconsistent with the amended law be passed.
issues.conclusion: The provision requiring decrees to conform to the amended law operated retrospectively. The decrees based on the deleted right could not be sustained and were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, as amended by Punjab Act 10 of 1960, operates retrospectively and applies in pending appellate proceedings. Under Ram Sarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 858, its language requires an appellate court to give effect to the substantive provisions of the amendment, whether the appeal is against a decree granting or refusing pre-emption.

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: A pre-emption suit is pending before an appellate court.
predicates.prior_preemption_right_removed: An amendment removes the category of pre-emption right recognized when the claim was decided below.
predicates.decree_based_on_prior_right: The decree under appeal rests on the removed category of pre-emption right.

issues.definition: When a pre-emption appeal is pending, the relied-on right has been removed, and the decree rests on that right, the decree cannot stand.

issues.legal_issue: The retrospective operation of an amendment that both removes former pre-emption rights and creates a new tenant-based right requires the new right to be treated as vested at the relevant time, allowing claimants who assert the qualifying tenancy to amend their claims and prove that right on remand.
material_facts: The respondents’ original claims relied on pre-emption rights that the amendment deleted.
The amendment created a right of pre-emption for tenants holding the sold land or part of it under tenancy of the vendor.
The respondents asserted that they were tenants of the lands in suit and sought an opportunity to claim under the new provision; their tenancy-based entitlement had not been tried.
issues.conclusion: The new substantive right operated retrospectively along with the provision governing pending decrees. The respondents were entitled on remand to amend their claims and attempt to prove their entitlement as tenants.
issues.legal_principle: The retrospective operation of section 31 necessarily gives retrospective effect to the substantive provisions of amended section 15, including both the extinction of former rights and the creation of new rights. Although a pre-emptor ordinarily must possess the right at the time of sale, suit, and decree, the retrospective statutory effect deems a qualifying new right to have vested at the relevant time. The applicable provisions were sections 31 and 15(1)(c), clause 4, of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, as amended by Punjab Act 10 of 1960; Ram Sarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 858, supports the retrospective effect of section 31.

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: A pre-emption suit is pending before an appellate court.
predicates.new_tenant_preemption_right_created: An amendment creates a pre-emption right for a tenant of the sold land or part of it under the vendor.
predicates.claimant_asserts_qualifying_tenancy: The claimant asserts that they held the sold land or part of it under tenancy of the vendor.

issues.definition: When an appeal in a pre-emption suit is pending, an amendment creates a tenant-based right, and the claimant asserts the required tenancy, the claimant may amend the claim and prove that right on remand.
